title: Is Improving Schools from the Bottom Up the Key to Real Reform?
author: Frederick Hess
summary: Frederick Hess reviews A Chance to Solve Their Own Problems by Jal Mehta and colleagues, a study of 'continuous improvement and design' (CID) approaches such as Instructional Rounds, Data Wise and Lesson Study in K-12 schools. The authors profile four long-running initiatives, drawing on more than 350 interviews, and explain why Deming-style methods give uneven results when goals are unclear, workflows are unpredictable and measurement is imprecise. Hess praises their diagnosis of culture, political dynamics, professional isolation and misaligned incentives, and the candid teacher complaints that reveal why reforms fail. He remains a skeptic of CID, concluding that its methods are poorly suited to the turbulence of American schools, which echoes his earlier argument about dysfunctional system leadership. He finds the prescriptive final chapter jargon-heavy and weaker than the descriptive sections, but credits the book for practical wisdom about the how of school improvement.
points: Continuous improvement and design strategies have received little scrutiny, and the book is one of the first to test whether they work.
The reasons for uneven results include unclear goals, unpredictable workflows and imprecise measurement of outcomes.
Teacher complaints about data collection, exit tickets and the fear of being judged reveal how small frustrations undo reform efforts.
Teachers like coaching and collaboration that feel supportive and unhassled, but Hess questions whether genial support produces results.
Hess's bottom line is that CID needs time and predictability that schools hit by shifting priorities, turnover and overload rarely have.
quotes: Whole shelves of edu-books promise, “If you just DO THIS, students will learn!” From growth mindset to inquiry-based learning, methods claiming to be the secret ingredient of successful schools have been peddled by a slew of authors.
Although they are clearly CID enthusiasts, they observe that these acclaimed strategies have received little scrutiny. No one has spent much time or energy figuring out if they actually work.
The book is at its best when unpacking how culture, political dynamics, professional isolation, tight timelines, and misaligned incentives play out.
Indeed, the book’s most revealing contributions show up in the candid expressions of snark by educators who feel threatened, condescended to, or overburdened by these “teacher-centered” efforts.
Now, it’s no surprise that teachers prefer improvement strategies that feel supportive. They like coaching when it’s unobtrusive, convenient, and focused on their priorities.

For me, Mehta et al.’s bottom line is this: CID asks educators to use methods that are poorly suited to the culture and turbulence of America’s K–12 systems. Changing mindsets, routines, and practice requires time and predictability.

Almost three decades ago, I argued in Spinning Wheels that the disappointing track record of so many school reforms isn’t necessarily about the particular policies but the chaotic, dysfunctional dynamics of system leadership.
The prescriptive sections are weaker than the descriptive ones. It’s easier to diagnose obstacles than to surmount them.
